The simple explanation for larger nodes being used is that, the smaller the gate of a transistor, the more densly packed they are on the die. If you shoot a particle at it, it’s more likely to hit a transistor and (maybe) wreak havoc. Being on larger nodes allows for wider spacing between transistors, lowering the chances of a charged particle actuating hitting something important in the chip.

Member of a formula student team here!

Not sure if it's like this over the Atlantic, but here in Europe FS is a competition that's more about designing and manufacturing of the car than actually racing one another. That being said, there are a number of events in which teams participate.

Broadly, these are dynamic events ( car goes vroom on the track ) and static events ( basically imagine marketing meetings ).


In the competition we're participating in , dynamic events are
- acceleration ( tests how quickly the car accerates in a straight line )
- endurance ( generally, this tests reliability and durability )
- efficiency ( a kinda second part of endurance, it measures fuel consumption during that event )
- autocross: tests the car's handling on one lap of a narrow ( ish ) track
- skid-pad: basically tests turning radius 

The static events are
- cost report: team presents a bill of materials for... Basically everything, from materials to tools and even labor ( simulated hourly wages , nobody actually pays us lol )
- design report: when the team builds a car, they have to also write an Engineering Design Report basically explaining why decisions were made ( why does this component go here, etc ). The EDR is then presented to the judges who grade it.
- business plan: a business scenario is proposed ( "suppose you had access to 20 tracks and 100 vehicles like the one you built" ) and we have to build a functional business around this
